## Design

### 2026-10-08 – During the PCB design process, the initial 50 mm × 50 mm layout and corner mounting hole placements worked well for mechanical stability, but several electrical layout issues arose. Running the high-s

**3h**

During the PCB design process, the initial 50 mm × 50 mm layout and corner mounting hole placements worked well for mechanical stability, but several electrical layout issues arose. Running the high-speed SPI signal traces (MOSI, MISO, SCK) too close to one another without adequate grounding caused cross-talk and signal noise during file transfers, requiring the addition of a bottom-layer ground plane and wider trace spacing. Additionally, using standard thin 10 mil traces for the 5V and 3.3V power rails resulted in voltage drops during SD card write operations, which triggered brownout resets on the ESP32; widening these power traces to 25 mil resolved the power delivery issues. Finally, generic MicroSD breakout modules caused footprint misalignment due to non-standard pin configurations, which was solved by standardizing the layout around a 0.1-inch header footprint to ensure reliable connections.

### 2026-10-08 – In the second three-hour session, component layout and electrical stability improved significantly as placing the MicroSD card socket along the board edge provided easy physical access, while a bottom

**4h**

In the second three-hour session, component layout and electrical stability improved significantly as placing the MicroSD card socket along the board edge provided easy physical access, while a bottom-layer ground pour successfully shielded the SPI lines from signal interference and 25-mil power traces resolved current drops. However, several manufacturing and layout errors were encountered during rule checks. Widening the power traces created tight DRC clearance violations around the 0.1-inch header pads, requiring local trace necking to maintain proper spacing. Additionally, silkscreen pin labels were overlapping copper pads, and solid copper ground plane connections on header pads lacked thermal relief spokes—both of which were corrected by repositioning text layers and enabling thermal relief legs to prevent heat-sink issues during hand soldering.

During the final two hours of the design session, focus shifted to final verification, export preparation, and documentation cleanup. The design underwent a rigorous, error-free Design Rule Check (DRC) pass to confirm that all clearance, net, and polygon connect violations were fully resolved. The Gerber and Excellon drill files were then packaged into a production-ready ZIP archive, and the final 3D rendering views were exported to verify component clearances, silkscreen legibility, and board geometry one last time before submitting the files to the fabrication facility.

### 2026-10-08 – Over the course of the next five hours, attention transitioned from final CAD cleanup into active hardware staging, firmware loading, and system validation. You began by flashing the compiled main.ino

**5h**

Over the course of the next five hours, attention transitioned from final CAD cleanup into active hardware staging, firmware loading, and system validation. You began by flashing the compiled main.ino firmware onto the ESP32 and configuring the SPI interface for the MicroSD storage module. Next, you wired up the physical prototype on your workbench to test power stability, ensuring the 3.3V regulator prevented the brownout resets previously encountered during heavy write operations. Finally, you conducted read and write stress tests over the local network connection, verifying that files could be uploaded and accessed seamlessly through the mobile and PC interface to mark the complete success of the Hack Life storage server project.
